The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) validates a foundational, high-level understanding of the AWS Cloud. It is aimed at candidates with roughly six months of exposure to AWS in any role (technical, managerial, sales, purchasing or financial).

The scored content is weighted across four domains:

  • Domain 1 — Cloud Concepts: 24%
  • Domain 2 — Security and Compliance: 30%
  • Domain 3 — Cloud Technology and Services: 34%
  • Domain 4 — Billing, Pricing, and Support: 12%

Questions are multiple choice (one correct answer) or multiple response (two or more correct answers). Always check the official exam guide for the current format, length and passing score.

AWS describes six advantages of cloud computing:

  • Trade fixed expense for variable expense
  • Benefit from massive economies of scale
  • Stop guessing capacity
  • Increase speed and agility
  • Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
  • Go global in minutes

Key ideas: elasticity (scale out and in with demand), high availability across Availability Zones, and paying only for what you use.

The Well-Architected Framework has six pillars:

  • Operational Excellence
  • Security
  • Reliability
  • Performance Efficiency
  • Cost Optimization
  • Sustainability

Cloud migration guidance is captured in the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF), whose perspectives are Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations.

AWS is responsible for security of the cloud — the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run AWS services. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud — their data, identity and access management, operating system patching on EC2, network and firewall configuration, and encryption choices.

The split shifts with the service: for EC2 (IaaS) you patch the guest OS; for managed services such as Amazon RDS or AWS Lambda, AWS takes on more of the stack.

AWS IAM controls who can do what in your account:

  • Protect the root user with MFA and use it only for the few tasks that require it
  • Grant least privilege through IAM policies
  • Use IAM roles for applications and AWS services instead of long-term access keys
  • Use AWS IAM Identity Center for workforce single sign-on across accounts

Related services: AWS Organizations (multi-account management with service control policies), AWS Artifact (compliance reports), Amazon GuardDuty (threat detection), AWS Shield (DDoS protection), AWS WAF (web application firewall), AWS KMS (encryption keys).

An AWS Region is a separate geographic area containing multiple, isolated Availability Zones (one or more discrete data centers each). Deploying across multiple AZs provides high availability. Edge locations serve Amazon CloudFront content and Route 53 DNS close to users.

Know what each core service is for:

  • Compute: Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda (serverless), Amazon ECS/EKS (containers), AWS Elastic Beanstalk
  • Storage: Amazon S3 (object), Amazon EBS (block for EC2), Amazon EFS (shared file), S3 Glacier storage classes (archive)
  • Databases: Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora (relational), Amazon DynamoDB (NoSQL key-value), Amazon Redshift (data warehouse)
  • Networking: Amazon VPC, Amazon Route 53 (DNS), Amazon CloudFront (CDN), Elastic Load Balancing
  • Management: Amazon CloudWatch (metrics/logs), AWS CloudTrail (API activity audit), AWS Config (resource configuration history)

EC2 purchase options: On-Demand (no commitment), Savings Plans and Reserved Instances (1- or 3-year commitment for lower prices), Spot Instances (spare capacity at a large discount, can be interrupted) and Dedicated Hosts.

Cost tools: AWS Pricing Calculator (estimate before you build), AWS Cost Explorer (analyse spend), AWS Budgets (alerts on cost or usage), and the AWS Cost and Usage Report.

Support plans: Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise. AWS Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks; the full set of checks requires Business support or higher.
